title: Velocity + Margin Plays: lab notes and messaging experiments
content:
Purpose
--------
Working lab doc: collect concise, testable claim variants and micro-proof patterns we can use in field demos, battlecards, and measuring scripts. Focus is not on full narratives (that comes later) — this is a playbook of claim scaffolds + what to measure to validate them quickly.

Quick summary thesis
--------------------
Customers care about two practical things: (1) predictable response time for end-users (latency tail behavior and p95/P99), and (2) per-unit cost to serve production traffic (tokens, sessions, embeddings). Framing: velocity (ms perception) + margin (cost per session) => pick a small set of crisp, measurable claims that combine the two (e.g., "Under Xms median for single-turn search snippets while reducing tokens per session cost by Y% vs competitor baseline").

Primary audiences and use cases
--------------------------------
- Product/engineering evaluation: SRE/infra buyers who need latency SLOs and deterministic throughput
- Platform/infra leads: care about capacity planning and committed cost (Dedicated)
- Growth/Product: care about cost per active user/session and demo speed for PLG motion

Claim scaffolds (simple, testable)
---------------------------------
1) "Consistent interactive latency"
   - Claim: "P95 < 250ms for 64-token completions under steady-state 200 QPS"
   - Proof: real traffic replay + internal tracer waterfall (token-level timings) + SDR (service degradation report)

2) "Fast cold-starts & fast fallbacks"
   - Claim: "Cold starts limited to < 800ms for first request; fallback to smaller variant keeps time < 300ms"
   - Proof: synthetic cold-start tests across regions + canary failover trace showing fallback path latency

3) "Token-dollar efficiency"
   - Claim: "ms-per-dollar improvement: we deliver same median latency at 30% lower token cost vs competitor baseline for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) flows"
   - Proof: run identical prompts through both systems; normalize costs by our price and public competitor published price or estimate from their docs; show tokens-per-answer and latency distributions

4) "Tail-smoothing via batching + cache"
   - Claim: "Using prefix caching + micro-batching reduces P99 by X% and cost per 1k requests by Y% for conversational sessions with reuse rate > 35%"
   - Proof: controlled A/B with traffic patterns that emulate high reuse; measure caching hit rate and cost delta

Which numbers to use as hypotheses (for experiments)
---------------------------------------------------
- p50 target for demo-worthy interactivity: 40–80ms for small prompts (16–64 tokens)
- p95 target for production SLO: 200–400ms (depends on model size)
- p99 target for robust service: aim to be < 1s for single-turn flows
- cost deltas: conservative claim: 20% lower per-session cost; aggressive claim: 40% in high-amortization workloads

Measurements and instrumentation checklist
-----------------------------------------
- Traffic capture: replay traces and production sample of 48h (anonymized)
- Metrics: token-counts per session, request-latency-per-stage (ingress, model-generate, network), cache-hit rate, batch size distribution, GPU utilization, instance-hours per 100k requests
- Comparison baseline: publicly documented competitor pricing + community benchmarks (note unknown discounts — use conservative pricing assumptions and flag them)
- Error bars: run tests 3x across different cluster sizes and regions; capture median, p95, p99

Competitive notes (quick observations)
-------------------------------------
- Competitor A: often reports low median latency but lacks publicized caching and batching controls — their p99 can spike under bursty traffic. They price per-token aggressively but don't expose session-level amortization features.
- Competitor B: packaged as turn-key model hosting; good tail latency on small models but per-token cost increases steeply on longer context and multi-turn sessions. They do not offer turnkey KV prefix caching.
- Open-source self-hosted stacks: cost depends heavily on ops expertise; can beat us on raw $/token if customer uses large batch sizes and allows slow tail, but they rarely provide SLO-backed guarantees.

Messaging tradeoffs (wording + risk)
-----------------------------------
- Emphasize predictable SLOs rather than absolute ms numbers in top-of-funnel content (risk: literal ms numbers invite courtroom nitpick or pricing changes).
- Use sample scenarios (e.g., "search results for a news app, 64-token summary, 500 QPS traffic profile") for detailed claims in field collateral and RFP responses.
- For case studies, use customer-specific amortization and show “before/after” for cost per DAU/session rather than tokens/second to be tangible.

Sample one-liners (for hero copy & elevator)
-------------------------------------------
- "Same interactivity your users expect — at a fraction of the per-session cost."
- "SLO-backed latency at scale, without paying for idle GPUs."
- "Cut token spend on repeated context by up to 40% with automatic prefix caching."

Proof artifacts to prepare (ranking priority)
-------------------------------------------
1) Short reproducible benchmark scripts (python notebooks + sample dataset) that show p95/p99 deltas and cost calc; attach to PRs and sales demos. (linked -> github PR-321)
2) 2-page field-ready cheat sheet (metric definitions, measurement recipe, safe-phrases).
3) Demo recording (90s) showing baseline vs caching + batching on same workload.
4) Customer mini-case (anonymized) where we reduced per-session cost > 25% while meeting p95 SLOs.

Demo plan (minimal reproducible scenario)
----------------------------------------
- Workload: RAG search + summarization; prompt size 48–128 tokens; reuse rate 40% (simulate repeated contexts).
- Traffic shape: 5-minute ramp to steady 250 QPS, 20% burst spikes of +200% lasting 30s.
- Measurements: collect latency per stage, token counts, batch sizes, cache hits, pre/post cost estimate per 10k sessions.
- Success criteria: p95 under 350ms and cost per 10k sessions reduced by >= 20% vs baseline competitor run.

Field enablement snippets (for AE/CS)
-------------------------------------
- "If you're optimizing for interactive user experiences, focus on p95 — it's what your end-users notice. We design for predictable p95 and provide tooling to tune batching/caching to reduce cost without hurting p95."
- Quick ask: "Give us a 24–48h sample traffic dump (anonymized). We'll run a focused lab and return a 1-page findings + recommended knob changes you can apply in test."

Open questions / risks to validate
--------------------------------
- How to normalize competitor pricing safely when discounts and enterprise pricing are opaque? (Plan: use published list prices + note caveats; include sensitivity band).
- Does Dedicated autoscale policy add hidden costs in bursty workloads? Need to simulate reserved vs bursted capacity.
- Legal review: ensure claims that include % improvements have reproducibility notes and acceptable margins (e.g., "up to X%" or "typically X–Y% in our tests").

Next actions (owner + timeline)
-------------------------------
- Alyssa: draft 1-pager cheat sheet and hero claim language (by 2025-12-08).
- Marco: produce benchmark notebook and run 3-host replicates vs competitor baseline (by 2025-12-10).
- Leah: coordinate demo recording and AE playbook snippets (by 2025-12-12).
- Tomas: legal/growth review queue for claim phrasing and sensitivity band (by 2025-12-15).

Appendix: quick measurement recipes (copyable)
-----------------------------------------------
- ms-per-dollar calc: (total request latency sum in ms across period) / (estimated infra cost for the period in USD) => not customer-facing raw metric but useful to compare internal knob tradeoffs.
- session-amortization sample: show cost-per-session as (instance-hours cost * fraction used for workload) / number of sessions served in that period. Include assumptions about committed vs spot pricing.

Notes to self
-------------
Keep this doc terse and operational. The goal is to output (1) a reproducible lab notebook, (2) a 1-page field sheet, and (3) a 90s demo clip. Avoid political positioning here — focus on measurable, repeatable artifacts we can ship to AE/CS quickly.
